steps.title: Purpose and contributor
steps.introduction: Begin with what this contributor can reveal through experience, knowledge, action, memory, or relationship.

fields.label: Working film title
fields.help: Use a provisional title. It can change as the project develops.

fields.label: Contributor and story role
fields.help: Identify the person by role rather than private contact details. What do they know, do, want, remember, or risk?

fields.label: Purpose of this interview
fields.help: What could this encounter contribute to the film that cannot be gained from general background research alone?
fields.caution: Using the interview only to deliver information the film could explain elsewhere.

fields.label: What should the audience be able to understand or experience?
fields.help: Describe the audience need without scripting what the contributor must say.

steps.title: Static, dynamic, or combined strategy
steps.introduction: Choose the form by asking what the story needs the contributor to do. Static and dynamic are strategies, not hierarchies.

fields.label: Provisional interview form
fields.help: Choose the strategy that currently serves the story, contributor, access, and production conditions.

options.label: Static
options.description: Concentrate attention, reflection, framing, and clean sound.

options.label: Dynamic
options.description: Place speech inside action, movement, work, location, or encounter.

options.label: Combined
options.description: Use each strategy for a distinct story purpose.

options.label: Undecided
options.description: Name the test needed before making the choice.

fields.label: What does the story need the contributor to do?
fields.help: Will they reflect, remember, demonstrate, navigate, work, interact, revisit a place, or do something else observable?

fields.label: Why does this form serve the contributor and story?
fields.help: Connect the choice to attention, action, place, relationship, comfort, access, image, and sound.
fields.caution: Choosing movement only for visual variety or stillness only for convenience.

fields.label: What must you test before recording?
fields.help: Name a small test of location, movement, task, comfort, camera position, or sound that could confirm or revise the choice.

steps.title: Relationship, consent, and boundaries
steps.introduction: Contributor agency begins before recording. Explain the project and revisit consent as conditions change.

fields.label: Your relationship to the contributor
fields.help: How do you know them, and how might that position affect trust, access, expectation, power, or interpretation?

fields.label: What will you explain before recording?
fields.help: Describe how you will explain the project, likely use of the material, practical process, filmmaker presence, and meaningful choices.

fields.label: Topics, locations, people, or actions needing care
fields.help: Identify boundaries, vulnerability, privacy, safety, or changing circumstances that require a specific conversation.

fields.label: How will you check and revisit consent?
fields.help: Plan when and how you will confirm understanding, comfort, participation, and any agreed limits.

fields.label: Clear stop or change-direction condition
fields.help: Name a sign or circumstance that would make you pause, stop, move, change the question, or abandon the planned action.
fields.caution: Treating a signed form as permission to ignore discomfort or changing circumstances.

steps.title: Question route
steps.introduction: Build a map, not a script. Move from an open invitation toward specific events, sensory detail, and responsive follow-up.

fields.label: Opening invitation
fields.help: Write an open prompt that helps the contributor begin in their own terms.

fields.label: Specific event or moment
fields.help: Ask for an experience located in time and place rather than a general opinion.

fields.label: Detail prompt
fields.help: Invite concrete memory: what they noticed, heard, saw, felt, handled, or did.

fields.label: Responsive follow-ups
fields.help: Prepare useful prompts such as: What happened next? Where were you? Who else was present? What did you notice? Leave room to follow the contributor’s exact words.

fields.label: Action or place invitation
fields.help: If appropriate, ask whether they can show, demonstrate, revisit, or take you somewhere. Keep consent, safety, and accuracy visible.

fields.label: Closing invitation
fields.help: Give the contributor space to add, correct, qualify, or identify what the interview has missed.

steps.title: Listening and responsive direction
steps.introduction: Listening is the primary directing skill. Notice language, pauses, energy, contradiction, and openings into scenes.

fields.label: What will you listen and watch for?
fields.help: Choose the cues you want to keep active during the encounter.

options.label: Exact words or phrases worth following
Changes in energy, emotion, or certainty
References to people, places, objects, or events
Actions that could be shown or revisited

fields.label: How will you make room for silence?
fields.help: Describe how you will resist filling every pause with the next prepared question.

fields.label: How will the film acknowledge your presence?
fields.help: Will questions be heard? Will you be visible or interacting? Will the contributor answer in complete thoughts? Make the choice explicit.

fields.label: If an answer opens an unexpected scene…
fields.help: How will you decide whether to follow it, pause for clarification, return later, or protect a boundary?

steps.title: Image, movement, and sound plan
steps.introduction: Build the recording conditions before the first question. A usable answer depends on picture, sound, comfort, and safety.

fields.label: Framing and visual plan
fields.help: Describe camera distance, eyeline, background, light, body position, movement, and how the frame supports the contributor and story.

fields.label: If the interview moves: route and stopping points
fields.help: Plan the action, route, pace, transitions, stopping points, camera position, background activity, and safety. If static, explain why movement is unnecessary.

fields.label: Sound plan
fields.help: Choose the quietest workable location, microphone placement, headphone monitoring, room tone, and how you will handle clothing, traffic, ventilation, movement, or other noise.

fields.label: Before recording, confirm…
fields.help: Use this as a preparation check, not a score.

options.label: The contributor understands the project and current plan
Relevant boundaries and stop conditions are clear
Frame, eyeline, background, and light are intentional
Microphone is placed and monitored with headphones
Likely noise and interruptions have been checked
Time is planned for room tone or location atmosphere
Any route, action, or stopping points are achievable and safe

steps.title: Direction reflection and next action
steps.introduction: Test whether the plan creates conditions for discovery while protecting the contributor and the integrity of the film.

fields.label: What can this contributor reveal?
fields.help: Name the experience, knowledge, relationship, memory, decision, or process that gives the encounter value.

fields.label: What can the camera and microphone witness?
fields.help: Name observable action, behavior, place, sound, interaction, or change—not only an expected statement.

fields.label: What must your directing choices protect?
fields.help: Consider agency, consent, dignity, accuracy, comfort, safety, boundaries, and the audience’s understanding.

fields.label: Your next practical action
fields.help: State one achievable conversation, location test, sound test, question rehearsal, or access check to complete before recording.

fields.label: What part of the plan may need to change?
fields.help: Identify the assumption most likely to be revised when you meet the real contributor, location, action, or production condition.

teacherExample.contributorRole: The volunteer choir director leads an intergenerational community choir and makes practical decisions about rehearsal, confidence, blend, and performance readiness.
teacherExample.interviewPurpose: Reveal how the director listens, corrects, encourages, and carries responsibility for a group whose abilities and confidence vary.
teacherExample.audienceUnderstanding: Experience leadership as a series of attentive decisions rather than a general claim about the value of music.
teacherExample.storyNeed: The film needs the director both to reflect on responsibility and to demonstrate that responsibility through rehearsal decisions, gesture, correction, and listening.
teacherExample.formReason: A brief static encounter can support concentration and memory. Dynamic conversation during a simple rehearsal passage can reveal leadership through action and sound.
teacherExample.formTest: Record a short rehearsal sound test and walk the camera route without interviewing to confirm that voices remain intelligible and movement does not interrupt the choir.
teacherExample.relationship: The filmmaker has provisional access through the choir director. Participation by individual choir members requires separate discussion rather than being assumed.
teacherExample.projectExplanation: Explain the short course film, how rehearsal and interview material may be combined, whether questions will be heard, where the film may be shown, and that participation can be paused.
teacherExample.boundaries: Confirm which choir members wish to appear, whether any rehearsal material should remain private, and whether correction or difficulty creates discomfort for particular participants.
teacherExample.consentCheck: Confirm the plan before recording, check again before moving into rehearsal, and pause if a participant or the director signals concern.
teacherExample.stopCondition: Stop or redirect if a participant withdraws, a correction becomes personally sensitive, the planned movement obstructs rehearsal, or sound cannot be recorded without disrupting the group.
teacherExample.openInvitation: When you enter this room before rehearsal, what are you listening for?
teacherExample.specificEvent: Tell me about a rehearsal when the group suddenly began to sound different.
teacherExample.sensoryDetail: What did you hear that told you the singers had found it?
teacherExample.followUps: What happened just before that? What did you change? Who noticed first? What did you do next?
teacherExample.showPrompt: Would you be comfortable showing how you help the group find the opening note?
teacherExample.closingQuestion: What have I not asked that matters to how you lead this choir?
listeningCues: References to people, places, objects, or events
teacherExample.silencePlan: After a reflective answer, count a quiet beat before checking the question route. Let the director decide whether to continue or revise the answer.
teacherExample.filmmakerPresence: Questions may remain audible so the encounter is not presented as invisible observation. During rehearsal, prompts will be brief and will not compete with the director’s attention.
teacherExample.unexpectedAnswer: If the director refers to a sensitive moment involving a singer, pause and ask whether the topic should remain general, continue off camera, or stop.
teacherExample.visualPlan: Use a stable medium frame for reflection with a meaningful but uncluttered rehearsal background. During rehearsal, use restrained handheld or supported movement that keeps the director’s gestures and relationship to the group legible.
teacherExample.dynamicRoute: Begin beside the rehearsal circle, move only between songs, and establish two safe stopping positions that do not block singers or music stands.
teacherExample.soundPlan: Use a close microphone for the director, monitor continuously, test the room’s reverberation, record quiet room tone before singers arrive, and gather rehearsal atmosphere separately.
teacherExample.reveal: The director can reveal how care and authority operate through listening and small decisions.
teacherExample.witness: The camera can witness gesture, correction, repetition, interaction, and the group’s sound changing in response.
teacherExample.protect: The plan must protect voluntary participation, dignity during correction, rehearsal safety, musical accuracy, and the director’s ability to lead.
teacherExample.nextAction: Hold a contributor and location conversation, then complete a five-minute sound and route test without recording a formal interview.
teacherExample.revision: The dynamic section may need to become observational if conversation interferes with rehearsal or if the room makes usable speech impossible.

export.title: INTERVIEW DIRECTION PLAN
export.disclosure: Prepared with the DOC 515 Interview Direction Lab. This is a planning document, not proof of consent or permission.
